summary:
Trend Detective is a website for people who plan around a season, such as festival organisers, growers and local services. It answers one question: is my season really shifting, or were the last few years just unusual?

The user picks any place on a globe, the months that matter, and a variable (air temperature, coldest temperature, or rain and snow). The site pulls NASA’s monthly record for that point, plots it, and reports how fast it is changing, whether the change is statistically significant, and since when the evidence has been strong. If the evidence is not there yet, it estimates how many more years of data are needed.

This covers the challenge’s four objectives: choosing variables, acquiring data for a region, visualizing the time series, and testing the trend. It matters because the usual trend test is unreliable on climate data. It misses 45 years of warming in Seoul and raises false alarms in simulations. Every answer is therefore checked with a corrected test.
details:
Trend Detective answers one question for people who plan around a season, such as festival organisers, growers and local services: has my season really changed, or were the last few years just unusual?

  1. The user picks a place (a preset city or any point clicked on the globe).
    • a one-line verdict: rising, falling, tests disagree, or no clear shift yet
    • the rate of change per decade with a 95% confidence interval
    • the year since which the evidence has been strong (a slider replays the record year by year)
    • if there is no clear shift yet, an estimate of how many more years of data would be needed

How it works

The chosen months are averaged into one value per year, and that yearly series is tested in two ways:

  • Quick check: ordinary least squares with textbook standard errors, which is what most tools report.
  • Careful check: OLS with the standard error widened for autocorrelation (effective sample size, Santer et al. 2000), plus the Hamed-Rao modified Mann-Kendall test. A shift counts as real only if both give p < 0.05.

When the two checks disagree, the site explains why. For all-year records, the seasonal cycle is removed first. Satellite rainfall from NASA Giovanni (GPM IMERG) is used to cross-check the MERRA-2 rainfall for Seoul. The two correlate at 0.94 month to month and give the same verdict.

Validation

  • A simulation on 2,000 trendless series showed naive OLS raising false alarms in up to 52% of cases when the data are autocorrelated, against 3.9% to 5.8% for the careful check (target 5%).
  • On Seoul’s all-year temperature record, naive OLS found no trend (p = 0.21), while the careful check found +0.36 °C per decade (p < 0.001).
  • The statistics run in the browser in JavaScript. An automated check confirms they match the Python reference on 48 analyses.

Benefits and intended impact

A planner can tell a lasting shift from a run of odd years before committing money. For example, January in Hwacheon has warmed by 0.70 °C per decade, with strong evidence since 2022. Summer rain in Seoul shows no clear shift. Answers are free, work for any location, and come with the uncertainty stated. The site does not predict outcomes such as bloom dates, ice thickness or yields. It reports whether the weather in a season has shifted.

What makes it creative

  • It turns a significance test into a decision tool for a specific season and place.
  • It shows two tests side by side, so users can see when a standard answer can’t be trusted.
  • It replays the record to show when the evidence became strong.
  • It estimates how long a weak trend would take to confirm.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, pyMannKendall) for the reference statistics and simulation. JavaScript and globe.gl for the website. Data from the NASA POWER API and NASA Giovanni. Hosted on GitHub Pages. AI assistance (Claude) was used for brainstorming, code, documentation and slides, as described in the AI use field and the repository.

Factors considered

  • Each series is one MERRA-2 grid cell of about 50 km, not a weather station.
  • About 45 yearly values per season limits statistical power, so weak shifts often show “no clear shift yet”.
  • Testing many month combinations raises false alarms, so the site asks users to choose their months first.
  • Live checks depend on NASA’s service being available. Saved records load if it is down.
  • Only straight-line trends are tested.
